projects.title: Diabetic Patient Readmission Prediction
projects.pitch: Predicting 30-day hospital readmission for diabetic patients across 130 US hospitals, optimising for recall rather than accuracy.

story.question: Which diabetic inpatients are most likely to be back within 30 days, and which clinical signals carry that risk?
story.method: Dropped ID columns and features with more than 95% missing values, encoded categoricals and standardised numerics, then compared Logistic Regression, KNN, SVM, Random Forest and XGBoost on a 70/30 split with 5-fold cross-validation. SMOTE was tested and rejected because it overfit, so final models trained on the natural 11% positive rate.
story.finding: Random Forest gave the best recall and F1 balance (recall 0.56) without overfitting. Lab procedure count, the three diagnosis codes, medication count and length of stay were the strongest predictors. Clinical variables beat demographics throughout.

signature.title: Readmission within 30 days by prior inpatient visits
signature.description: Share of encounters readmitted within 30 days, by the number of inpatient visits in the preceding year, computed from diabetic_data.csv. The baseline rate across all encounters is drawn as a reference line.

visuals.alt: Horizontal bar chart titled Top Features for Predicting Readmission Within 30 Days. Number of lab procedures, diagnosis codes 2, 1 and 3, and number of medications lead, each near 0.1 importance; number of outpatient visits trails at about 0.02.
visuals.caption: Random Forest feature importance for 30-day readmission.

visuals.alt: Correlation matrix heatmap of the diabetes dataset. Strongest off-diagonal relationships are admission type with admission source (0.48) and time in hospital with number of medications (0.48).
visuals.caption: Correlation matrix of numeric features before modelling.

links.label: Strack et al. 2014, HbA1c and readmissions

projects.title: Diabetes Risk and Management Dashboard
projects.pitch: A Power BI dashboard over 1,879 patient records asking which modifiable factors drive diabetes diagnosis and day-to-day management.

data.name: Diabetes health dataset
data.source: Kaggle (inferred from column schema and the Confidential DoctorInCharge field)

story.question: Of quality of life, diet quality, blood pressure, cholesterol risk, socioeconomic status and medication adherence, which matter most for developing and managing diabetes?
story.method: Recoded every binary flag into labelled categories, then built derived features: age bands, BMI risk level, blood pressure category, blood sugar category, renal function and cholesterol risk. Six dashboard panels slice the diagnosis outcome by each candidate factor with education and risk-level filters.
story.finding: Diet quality and medication adherence are the most direct, modifiable levers. Poor quality of life carried the highest diagnosis count (789), and middle and low socioeconomic groups accounted for over 70% of diagnoses. Blood pressure on its own did not separate diabetics from non-diabetics.

signature.title: Diagnosis rate by diet quality and BMI class
signature.description: Share of patients diagnosed with diabetes in each diet-quality and BMI cell, computed from diabetes_data.csv.

visuals.alt: Power BI dashboard titled Diabetes Risk/Management Insights with six panels: diagnoses by quality of life (poor 789, moderate 565, good 525), a diet-quality donut, diagnosis by blood pressure category, cholesterol risk against blood sugar, a socioeconomic status pie, and medication adherence by blood sugar category.
visuals.caption: The six-panel Power BI dashboard.

projects.title: New Jersey Load Prediction
projects.pitch: Forecasting hourly electricity demand for New Jersey's four utilities from weather and calendar features with LightGBM.

data.name: Utility hourly load, hourly weather, EIA generation and BEA economic series
data.source: PJM / utility CIEP and RSCP eligible hourly load files (August 2024 update), hourly weather for Newark and Vineland 2019 to 2024, EIA net generation, BEA and BLS economic indicators
data.records: 4 utilities x 2 rate classes, hourly 2019 to 2024
files: New Jersey Load Prediction Project/Cleaned utility Code/JCPL.zip
New Jersey Load Prediction Project/Cleaned utility Code/PSEG.zip
New Jersey Load Prediction Project/Cleaned utility Code/Project-ACE-complete.zip
New Jersey Load Prediction Project/Cleaned utility Code/Project-RECO-complete.zip

story.question: Can weather and calendar data alone forecast hourly load for JCP&L, PSE&G, Atlantic City Electric and Rockland Electric, and which inputs matter most?
story.method: Cleaned hourly weather in R (imputation, interpolation, outlier review), joined it to utility load by rate class and a hand-built date category table, then trained LightGBM regressors per utility and class after trialling linear regression and neural networks. Economic and renewable generation series were profiled for later inclusion.
story.finding: Atmospheric pressure, temperature and humidity dominate feature importance in every model; among calendar features weekday beats season. Load peaks between 2 pm and 4 pm and in June through September. Held-out scores lag training scores, so hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation are the stated next steps.

signature.description: Mean temperature by month and hour of day for Newark in 2023, computed from the hourly weather CSV inside the JCPL archive. The same diurnal and seasonal shape drives the load models.

projects.title: Medicare 2017 Payment Analysis
projects.pitch: What drives the gap between what Medicare pays and what hospitals collect? A Power BI exploration of 2017 inpatient charge data by region, DRG and provider.

data.name: Medicare Inpatient Hospitals by Provider and Service, 2017
data.source: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
data.records: Provider by DRG rows for 2017, with discharges, covered charges, total and Medicare payments

story.question: How do hospital referral region, DRG definition and provider state shape average total Medicare payments?
story.method: Cleaned the CMS charge file, then built a dashboard with a Key Influencers visual, a state choropleth, provider and referral-region rankings and dynamic filters. Regression and correlation checks backed the visual findings.
story.finding: DRG is the largest lever: heart transplant and heart assist implant cases raise average total payments by roughly $253.5K. Average Medicare payment sits near $11.8K against $13.98K average total payment, and specialised providers such as US Pain and Spine Hospital in Houston top the provider ranking at $72K. Chicago generates the most referrals, Washington the fewest.

signature.title: Average total payment by provider state
signature.description: Discharge-weighted average total payment per state, computed from Medicare Inpatient 2017.xlsx. Top fifteen states shown.

visuals.alt: Power BI dashboard titled Medicare 2017 Charges. Panels show average total payments by provider name led by US Pain and Spine Hospital at 72K, a gauge of 13.98K average total payments, hospital referrals by city led by Chicago with 26, three KPI cards (61.17K covered charges, 11.82K Medicare payments, 13.98K total payments), a US state map, and a Key Influencers panel.
visuals.caption: The Medicare 2017 Charges dashboard.

inferred: The README quotes $11,000 Medicare and $27,960 total payment; the dashboard cards read $11.82K and $13.98K. The site shows the dashboard values and flags the discrepancy here. The $27.96K figure appears to be the gauge maximum, which is twice the mean.

projects.title: Self-Determination Theory and Workplace Well-Being
projects.pitch: Do autonomy, relatedness and competence at work predict positive affect? A three-way ANOVA on 2,344 MIDUS participants.

data.name: Midlife in the United States (MIDUS)
data.source: MIDUS national longitudinal study, workplace and affect items
files: Self Determination Theory Project/Final SDT Code/categorizedFinal_cleaned_data.csv

story.question: Does workplace autonomy (decision authority), relatedness (coworker support) and competence (persistence in goal striving) influence employees' positive affect, and do the three interact?
story.method: Built composite scales for each construct, recoded them to low, medium and high, confirmed all 27 treatment cells were populated, and fitted a three-way ANOVA in R. Sex was dropped as a block after it interacted with a primary factor. The unusualness threshold was set at 0.12 given the exploratory aim.
story.finding: Competence (F = 14.79, p < 0.0001) and relatedness (F = 11.94, p < 0.0001) each raise positive affect; autonomy is weaker (p = 0.1036, partial eta squared 0.002). No two-way or three-way interactions were significant, so the three needs act independently.

signature.title: Positive affect by level of each need
signature.description: Mean positive affect with interquartile range at low, medium and high levels of autonomy, relatedness and competence, computed from the cleaned MIDUS extract.

visuals.alt: Histogram of positive affect by autonomy level. High-autonomy respondents cluster at positive affect 3.5 to 4, with counts above 400; low-autonomy respondents are few and spread across 2 to 4.
visuals.caption: Positive affect distribution by autonomy level, from the project report.

visuals.alt: ANOVA omnibus table. Competence F 14.793 p < 0.0001; relatedness F 11.937 p < 0.0001; autonomy F 2.269 p 0.1036; all interaction terms p > 0.4; residual df 2,317.
visuals.caption: ANOVA omnibus test.

links.label: Szulawski et al. 2021, Is self-determination good for your effectiveness?

inferred: ggplot2 is inferred from the histogram styling; no R script is committed, only the cleaned CSV.

The cleaned CSV stores each need as a survey frequency label rather than the numeric composite. The signature chart maps Never and Rarely (or Not at all and A little) to low, Some of the time (or Some) to medium, and Most or All of the time (or A lot) to high.

projects.title: Study Abroad Programs: PSU and OSU Integrated
projects.pitch: Scraping, cleaning and unifying two universities' study abroad catalogues into one queryable SQLite schema.

data.name: PSU and OSU study abroad program listings
data.source: Public program tables on the Penn State and Ohio State education abroad websites, scraped
data.records: 277 distinct program rows (554 rows in the committed CSV)
files: Study Abroad Programs Project/Cleaned Combined Code/PSU-OSU-COMBINED-FINAL.csv

story.question: Can two universities' study abroad catalogues be merged into one schema that answers where programs run, who offers them and how the portfolios differ?
story.method: Scraped program name, city, country and region with Beautiful Soup, normalised multi-city and multi-country entries, stripped formatting noise, added a College column, then loaded a mediated schema into SQLite and validated it with queries.
story.finding: Europe dominates with more than half of all programs; Asia and Latin America follow at roughly a tenth each. OSU leans on the United Kingdom while PSU concentrates on Australia and Argentina, and London alone hosts six programs.
